column1: # G7 phase 5: the overlay patch verb (`aontu set`)
# (docs/capability-review/g7-machine-access.md). Columns:
# name<TAB>patch<TAB>entry<TAB>input<TAB>expect, where input is a
# JSON object {overlay, set} -- the overlay text as it stands and
# the assignments to append -- and expect is the report:
# {appended, overlay, verdict} plus `codes` when there are findings.
# Messages are excluded, as every other verb's goldens exclude them.
# An overlay entry is just another CONJUNCT, and unification is
# order-independent, so appending to a second file is the same value
# as writing into the first. What it cannot do is change a PINNED
# value (patch-pinned-conflict): the lattice refuses, the verdict is
# invalid, and `why` locates the pinning site. The verdict is vet's,
# unchanged.
# So are the FINDINGS. An entry that will not parse is a broken
# schema as far as vet is concerned, and the report carries the
# parser's own code with the verdict (patch-entry-unparseable): the
# verb tells the caller which file it could not read and why, rather
# than `error` and nothing (test/spec/vet.tsv, vet-schema-*).
# Keys are QUOTED in the flattened line: a path segment may be a
# word the grammar spells otherwise (patch-keyword-key), a number
# (patch-numeric-key), or hold a space.
# Every expectation was obtained by the parity probe (AGENTS.md).

# IN-PLACE REPLACE (`aontu set --in-place`), riding `inPlace` on the
# input object. G7 deferred this behind a comment-preserving CST; it
# needs none, because a targeted span splice SERIALISES NOTHING -- it
# replaces `len` code units at one offset and every other byte, comment
# and blank line included, is untouched because it is never read
# (patch-inplace-keeps-comments pins exactly that).
# WHAT MAKES IT SAFE IS THE ROUND TRIP, not the `literal` role. A site
# names the TOKEN it points at, so a COMPOUND value reports its OPENING
# token while its canon is the whole thing: `min(1)` is a literal-role
# contribution whose src is `min`, `1+2` reports `1`, `{b:1}` reports
# `{`, `[1,2]` reports `[`, `1|2` reports `1`. Splicing any of those
# writes the new value INTO the expression -- `a: 5(1)`, `a: 5+2` --
# which is the canon-length corruption class reached by another route.
# So the src is parsed ALONE and required to mean the contribution's
# own canon. That is decided by the same unifier that made the
# contribution, so it cannot drift from it, and it gets the interesting
# case right without naming it: `0x1F` canons to `31`, which is not its
# own spelling but IS the contribution's canon, so a hex literal is
# editable (patch-inplace-hex-literal) while `min` is not
# (patch-inplace-call-refused).
# NEVER WORSE THAN APPEND. Where the value is not a single editable
# literal in this overlay, the assignment is APPENDED exactly as it
# would have been without the flag, plus one WARNING naming the case --
# and warnings never move a verdict. Both runners assert this for every
# row here by re-running it without the flag and requiring a verdict at
# least as good, so the claim is measured rather than stated.
# An ABSTRACT contribution (`a: integer`, `a: above(0)`) is refused for
# a different reason than a compound: it would not corrupt anything, it
# would DISCARD a constraint the author wrote, and appending already
# narrows it. A PREFERENCE is refused with no finding at all, because
# appending overrides a default correctly and nothing went wrong.
# Every expectation was obtained by the parity probe (AGENTS.md).

patch-inplace-keeps-comments
